title: Running Away from Running Records
author: Rachael Gabriel
summary: Reading researcher Rachael Gabriel argues that schools abandoning Running Records is less a verdict on the assessment than an indictment of educator professional development. She distinguishes levels of use: novice teachers just record and count errors, intermediate users categorise errors, and advanced users read the record as a replayable representation and solve for how the child arrived at the word, which is miscue analysis rather than error analysis. Her position is that novice and intermediate Running Records may not be worth the time, since simply listening to children read is enough, while advanced use is a missing piece of intervention because it makes instruction precise and responsive. She describes helping revise the Running Record form with expert Reading Recovery teachers and uses a martial arts analogy to explain why basic forms hide expert depth. She concludes that teachers are left in the messy middle without infrastructure for learning.
points: The retreat from Running Records reflects weak professional development more than flaws in the practice.
Counting errors is not miscue analysis; the point is to understand how the reader arrived at the word and what information they used or ignored.
For most classroom teachers, listening to children read is enough, and checkmarks and counts may be a distraction.
Advanced use can pinpoint what to teach next in ways universal screeners and WCPM scores cannot.
Developing expertise takes mentorship and intensive study over time, which current training such as LETRS does not provide.
quotes: The fact that so many schools are running away from Running Records (RRs) right now is not about problems with an assessment practice, or a set of ideas, a theory, a review, a policy or a law. It’s an indictment of the state of educator professional development.

This is why more testing in schools has not led to better achievement: not all assessment data is useful for teaching. RRs can be, but don’t have to be, and whether they are has everything to do with our imagination about the value of students’ thinking and the importance of teacher learning.

A novice or intermediate level RR is probably not worth the time. We can get what we need from simply listening to children read without marking checks and circles or coding the discrepancies the oral and written record.
Miscue analysis asks: How did you get to the word you said? What did you notice, use, try, infer and why?

Knowing the type of error just tells us the category of item to teach, but so much of learning to read isn’t just item knowledge, it’s strategies for efficiently accessing and integrating item knowledge to make a sentence make sense.
It’s really very simple, and we’re missing the whole point if we don’t listen to kids read. We don’t have to make checks or count errors.

It’s also not elitist magical thinking to believe there’s more to know about teaching and learning than social media sound bytes, online modules and 90minute workshops. It’s actually respect for the profession and its humans to acknowledge there’s more.
